tur39-1: Symptoms usually start within 24 hours, but can be delayed by up to 3 weeks. Mild symptoms can last up to 2 weeks; most symptoms settle within 2–4 weeks, though some can take longer.
tur39-2: One of the studies behind these recommendations was carried out in the USA and Canada with 103 young athletes: within the first 10 days, half of those doing about 20 minutes of aerobic exercise a day at an intensity that did not worsen symptoms (80% of the heart rate at which symptoms increased on a treadmill test) had recovered within 13 days, and half of those doing stretching only within 17 days (median time). Recovery took longer than 30 days in 2 of 52 people in the exercise group and 7 of 51 in the stretching group; however, this difference was not statistically significant. The studies were mostly done in young athletes; the evidence is more limited in adults and in non-sport injuries.
tur39-3: Stand next to a wall. First stand for 10 seconds with one foot slightly in front of the other, then swap feet. When this becomes easy, with someone beside you, walk along a corridor placing the heel of one foot against the toes of the front foot.
tur39-4: When you feel better, starting with short periods. England's grassroots sport guidance puts returning to school and work before returning to sport: once you have no symptoms at rest, usually around week 2, you can return to school or work part-time. During this period you can ask for adjustments such as half days or scheduled breaks.
tur39-5: Light aerobic exercise can help. In a study of 103 young people aged 13–18 with a sport-related concussion, half of those who started within the first 10 days and did about 20 minutes of walking or stationary cycling a day, at an intensity that did not worsen symptoms, had recovered within 13 days (median time); in those doing stretching only this was 17 days. Exercise intensity should increase your symptoms only mildly at most.
tur39-6: If symptoms do not improve within 2 weeks or get worse, see your doctor; if they last more than 4 weeks, an assessment by several specialties is recommended. If dizziness, neck pain or headache lasts more than 10 days, the international consensus recommends neck and balance (cervicovestibular) rehabilitation. In a small study of 31 people aged 12–30 whose dizziness, neck pain or headache persisted after a sport-related concussion, 73% of those who received this rehabilitation were cleared to return to sport within 8 weeks, compared with 7% of those who received general physiotherapy only (postural education, range-of-motion exercises, graded exertion).
tur39-7: After a heart attack, a stent or bypass surgery, many people are afraid to move. Yet properly adjusted exercise is part of treatment: in a review of 107 studies, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation reduced the risk of another heart attack and of hospital admission. The programme starts with your cardiologist's approval and progresses step by step.
tur39-8: Reduction in the risk of another heart attack at 6–12 months with cardiac rehabilitation (25 studies, 8,584 people)
tur39-9: Likely reduction in the risk of hospital admission at 6–12 months in the same review
tur39-10: The Cochrane review updated in 2026 looked at 107 randomised controlled trials involving 26,886 people with coronary heart disease; most participants had had a heart attack or a procedure to open the arteries (stent, bypass). At 6–12 months, exercise-based rehabilitation reduced the risk of another heart attack by 28% (about one heart attack prevented for every 71 people), and probably reduces the risk of hospital admission by about 35% (roughly one admission for every 17 people). A small reduction in deaths seems possible, but this result is not certain. Only 17% of participants were women.
tur39-11: Yes, when done with your cardiologist's approval and gradually. In a review of 107 studies, people taking part in exercise-based rehabilitation had fewer repeat heart attacks and hospital admissions. Your doctor decides how hard you should start.
tur39-12: A review of 24 studies (3,046 people) found that home programmes supported by health professionals and centre-based programmes were similarly effective. Choose the one you can keep attending regularly; a home programme also needs your doctor's approval and regular follow-up. According to the UK national audit of cardiac rehabilitation, about 70–80% of those who start a programme complete it; the NHS Long Term Plan (2019) aims for 85% of people with acute coronary syndrome (heart attack or unstable angina) to take part. In a US study that followed 1,120 people referred to cardiac rehabilitation for about 4 years, the death rate was 12% in those who took part in a home-based programme and 20% in those who did not; because this was an observational study, other factors may have played a part.

tur39-14: Start with 5–10 minutes; aim for 30 minutes on at least 3–5 days a week
tur39-15: In a 2023 Cochrane review combining 60 studies, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation was beneficial in centre-based, home-based (including digitally supported) and hybrid programmes. The European Society of Cardiology recommends that a supervised programme be considered for people with more severe disease, frailty or other conditions. You can choose whichever you can keep attending regularly; a home programme also needs your doctor's approval and follow-up.
